text: A chatbot that only talks has a bounded failure mode: a successful injection makes it say something it shouldn't. An agent — an LLM wired up with tool use so it can query a database, send an email, or call an internal API — has a completely different failure mode. The previous three lessons established you can't reliably stop every injection at the input layer. This lesson is about making sure that even when one succeeds, there's nothing much it can actually do.

You already know this principle from everywhere else in security: a service account gets the minimum access its task requires, nothing more, because every extra permission is pure downside risk. Apply that to an agent directly. An agent that only reads calendar availability shouldn't be able to delete events. An agent that drafts replies shouldn't send them unsupervised. The question for every tool you wire up is whether this specific task strictly requires it — not whether it would be useful.

That turns into concrete patterns. Scoped, short-lived credentials instead of one broad service account for the whole AI system. Read and write access kept on separate tools, so summarizing a mailbox doesn't imply the ability to send from it. An explicit, named allow-list of callable functions instead of general shell or API access — if a capability isn't on that list, the model has no path to it no matter what an injected instruction tells it to do.

Add output validation right before a tool call fires, checking the proposed action against what the user actually asked for. And for anything irreversible or high-impact, route it through a person first — the same human-in-the-loop approval gate already used for high-risk SOAR playbook actions earlier in this path. Sandbox execution where you can, and log every tool call in enough detail to reconstruct exactly what happened.

That's what makes privilege separation the most durable control in this chapter. It doesn't need to anticipate every clever phrasing, because the agent physically cannot perform an action it was never granted. It bounds the consequence of an attack instead of trying to guarantee the attack never succeeds — and that's the fight you can actually win.
